notes.meaning: Samson walks down from the hills to Timnah, a border town held by the Philistines, and notices a young woman there. His attraction begins a dangerous drift toward pagan culture, even though God's people were called to remain distinct. Following what appeals to the eyes often leads into temptation.

Samson returns home and asks his parents to arrange the marriage for him. In the ancient world, parents negotiated weddings and paid the bride price. Samson shows respect by involving his father and mother, but he is guided entirely by outward looks rather than godly character.

Samson's parents urge him to marry an Israelite woman rather than an uncircumcised foreigner outside of God's covenant. Circumcision was the physical mark showing that a man belonged to God's chosen people. Samson dismisses their wise advice and insists on her simply because she looks good to him.

Samson's parents do not realize that the Lord is actively at work behind the scenes. God does not force Samson to do wrong, but He overrules Samson's stubborn desires to create a clash with the Philistines. The Lord uses this human weakness to begin breaking the grip of an enemy that ruled over Israel.

Samson travels back to Timnah with his parents and reaches the local vineyards, where a young lion suddenly charges at him. The lion is in its youthful prime, fierce and dangerous. Lingering near vineyards was also spiritually risky for Samson, who had taken a Nazirite vow—a special dedication to God that included avoiding all grapes and wine.

The Spirit of the Lord rushes upon Samson, giving him sudden courage and incredible strength. Without any weapon, he tears the roaring beast apart as easily as a young goat. Samson keeps the victory entirely to himself, quietly trusting God without boasting about his power.

Samson continues down to the town and speaks with the young Philistine woman directly. Now that marriage negotiations have started, custom allows them to converse. Talking with her only confirms his initial desire to take her as his wife.

After some time passes, Samson returns to Timnah for the wedding and steps off the road to look at the lion's body. The hot sun has dried the carcass, leaving clean bones where a swarm of bees has built a hive. Finding sweet honey inside the remains of a fierce predator provides the idea for his coming riddle.

Samson scrapes out the honey, eats it along the road, and shares it with his parents. As a dedicated Nazirite, he was strictly forbidden from touching any dead body, making this a careless breach of his vow. He conceals where the honey came from so his parents can eat without feeling defiled.

Samson's father travels down for the formal marriage arrangements, and Samson hosts a standard wedding banquet. Such feasts normally lasted seven days with lively celebrations among the young men. Samson holds the party in the bride's hometown, willingly blending in with Philistine customs.

The Philistines assign thirty local men to attend the banquet alongside Samson. These men act as formal groomsmen, but they also serve as guards to watch over an imposing foreign guest. Samson has no companions of his own present, highlighting his isolation among his rivals.

Samson challenges the thirty guests with a riddle to be solved during the seven days of the feast. Riddles were a popular form of dinner entertainment and mental competition in the ancient world. The prize is steep, consisting of thirty linen undergarments and thirty costly suits of clothing.

Samson explains the stakes of the wager: if the guests fail to solve the riddle, they must give him the exact same clothing. The Philistine companions eagerly agree to the terms and ask to hear the puzzle. Confident in their numbers and wit, they walk straight into the contest.

Samson presents his riddle, declaring that food came out of the eater and sweetness out of the strong. The riddle describes the honey taken from the dead lion, an event only Samson knew about. Because the puzzle is based on private experience rather than common knowledge, the guests remain completely baffled for days.

Facing public disgrace and heavy financial loss, the Philistines turn to violence and threaten Samson's bride. They warn her that they will burn her and her father's house to the ground if she does not pry the secret out of Samson. Fear drives her to choose her people over loyalty to her husband.

Samson's bride weeps before him, accusing him of hating her because he has hidden the riddle's meaning. She uses emotional pressure to wear down his resistance. Samson defends himself by explaining that he has not even shared the answer with his own father and mother.

She weeps continuously through the feast until Samson finally yields on the seventh day because she pesters him so intensely. The man who could overpower a lion cannot stand up to the tears and begging of his bride. The moment she learns the secret, she passes it on to her countrymen.

Just before sunset on the last day, the Philistines boastfully give the answer by comparing sweetness to honey and strength to a lion. Samson immediately sees through their trick and uses a farming proverb to expose their deceit. He knows they could never have cracked the riddle without pressuring his wife.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church writers such as Ambrose saw the riddle as a divine mystery, picturing how the bitterness of death and danger was overcome to produce the sweetness of salvation.

notes.meaning: The Spirit of the Lord comes upon Samson with mighty strength, enabling him to strike down thirty Philistine men in the city of Ashkelon. He takes their garments to settle his wedding wager, fulfilling his word through the spoils of Israel's enemies. Burning with anger over the betrayal, Samson leaves the bride behind and returns to his family home.

Assuming Samson has completely abandoned the marriage, the bride's father gives her to Samson's chief groomsman. Giving a bride to the best man was a bitter insult that shattered any hope of reconciliation. This act of treachery creates an open breach that fuels the growing conflict between Samson and the Philistines.
